speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Despite elevated uncertainty, the economy is in a solid position.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains low, and the labor market is at or near maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has been running somewhat above our 2 percent longer-run objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We believe that the current stance of monetary policy leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that growth of economic activity has moderated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP rose at a 1.2 percent pace in the first half of this year, down from 2.5 percent last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although the increase in the second quarter was stronger at 3 percent, focusing on the first half of the year helps smooth through the volatility in the quarterly figures related to the unusual swings in net exports.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The moderation in growth largely reflects a slowdown in consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, business investment in equipment and intangibles picked up from last year’s pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Activity in the housing sector remains weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions have remained solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 150,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, remains low and has stayed in a narrow range over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wage growth has continued to moderate while still outpacing inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a wide set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are broadly in balance and consistent with maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.5 percent over the 12 months ending in June and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These readings are little changed from the beginning of the year, although the underlying composition of price changes has shifted: Services inflation has continued to ease, while increased tariffs are pushing up prices in some categories of goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have moved up, on balance, over the course of this year on news about tariffs, as reflected in both market-based and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond the next year or so, however, most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4¼ to 4½ percent and to continue reducing the size of our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to determine the appropriate stance of monetary policy based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Changes to government policies continue to evolve, and their effects on the economy remain uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Higher tariffs have begun to show through more clearly to prices of some goods, but their overall effects on economic activity and inflation remain to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A reasonable base case is that the effects on inflation could be short lived—reflecting a one-time shift in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it is also possible that the inflationary effects could instead be more persistent, and that is a risk to be assessed and managed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our obligation is to keep longer-term inflation expectations well anchored and to prevent a one-time increase in the price level from becoming an ongoing inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For the time being, we are well positioned to learn more about the likely course of the economy and the evolving balance of risks before adjusting our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see our current policy stance as appropriate to guard against inflation risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are also attentive to risks on the employment side of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In coming months, we will receive a good amount of data that will help inform our assessment of the balance of risks and the appropriate setting of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At this meeting, the Committee continued its discussions as part of our five-year review of our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We focused on potential revisions to our Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy and are on track to wrap up any modifications by late summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and price—stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Howard.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: There is a lot of “lean” in the markets and, not to mention, out of the Administration, for a rate cut now in September.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Is that expectation unrealistic at this point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, as you know, today we decided to leave our policy rate where it’s been, which—where I would characterize as modestly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is running a bit above 2 percent, as I mentioned, even excluding tariff effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market’s solid—historically low unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Financial conditions are accommodative, and the economy is not—the economy is not performing as though restrictive policy were holding it back inappropriately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it seems to, to me and to almost the whole Committee that the economy is not performing as though restrictive policy is holding it back inappropriately, and modestly restrictive policy seems appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All that said, there’s also downside risk to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In coming months, we’ll receive a good amount of data that will help inform our assessment of the balance of risks and the appropriate setting of the federal funds rate.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: So just to follow up: By, by “coming months,” does that include the possibility you’ll, you’ll be getting essentially two rounds of jobs and inflation data between now and the September meeting?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Is that potentially adequate to make a decision to lower rates at that point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do have—this is an, an, an intermeeting period when we’ll get two full rounds of employment and inflation data before the time of the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have made no decisions about September—we don’t do that in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll be taking that information into consideration and all the other information we get as we make our decision at the September meeting.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: You took out the word—or the notion that uncertainty has diminished from this statement.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Does that mean uncertainty has increased?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And I’m just wondering, the Administration has struck several deals with large trading partners where it seems like we now know what the rate is going to be.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Does knowing that rate add to your certainty to change policy, or do you need to wait to see the economic effects?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, essentially, the statement in the—in the—in our statement about uncertainty reflects what’s gone on since the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, at the time of the last meeting, uncertainty had, had, had moved down a little bit, but it was more or less even this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we took out, you know, “had diminished” because it didn’t diminish further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s not really much in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then your second question is—say again?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: There have been several deals that have been struck, and now we seem to have an idea of what the tariff rates are going to be with some of our large trading partners.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Does that not add to the kind of certainty you might need, or is it you’re waiting for the economic effects to show, show themselves?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, I think we’re still—so you’re right, it’s been a very dynamic time for these trade negotiations, and lots and lots of events in the intermeeting period, but we’re still, you know, a ways away from seeing where things settle down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are clearly getting more and more information.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I think at this point, people’s estimates, our estimates, outside estimates of the—of the likely, you know, effective, effective level of tariffs is, is not moving around that much at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But at the same time, there are many, many uncertainties left to resolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yes, we are learning more and more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t feel like we’re very close to the end of that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s not for us to judge, but it does—it feels like there’s much more to come, you know, as well looking ahead.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Neil.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Hi, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Neil Irwin with Axios.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: This morning, we got a GDP report in which final domestic private purchases decelerated—slowest pace since ’22.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: There was a weakness in the interest-sensitive sectors and residential investment, commercial structures.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Are those not signs that monetary policy is a little too restrictive right now, given current economic conditions?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the GDP and PDFP numbers came in pretty much right where we expected them to come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to look at the whole picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, certainly, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, economic activity data, GDP, private domestic final purchases—which we think is a narrower but better signal for future, for where the economy is going—has come down to a little better than 1 percent, 1.2 percent I think, in the case of GDP for the first half, whereas it was 2½ last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that has certainly come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you look at the labor market, what you see is, by many, many statistics, the labor market is kind of still in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s things like quits, you know, job openings, and—let alone the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re all very—by many measures, very similar to where they were a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you do not see a weakening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You do see a slowing in job creation, but also in a slowing—a slowing in the supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve got a labor market that’s in balance, albeit partially because both demand and supply for workers has—is coming down at the same pace, and that’s why the unemployment rate has remained roughly, roughly stable, which is why I said there—we do see downside risk in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, our two—our two mandate variables—right?—are inflation and maximum employment—stable prices and maximum employment, not so much growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the labor market looks, looks solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And even if you—if you look through the tariff effects, we think it’s still a bit above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s why our stance is where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, as I mentioned, you know, downside risks to the labor market are certainly apparent.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: So on labor, given the fluid labor supply situation, is there a number for this jobs report we get on Friday that would look to you like equilibrium job growth?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the, the main number you have to look at now is the unemployment rate, because if, if—it’s true that the, you know, demand for workers in the form of, let’s call it—say—just say, payroll jobs—that number has come down, but so has the breakeven number, kind of in tandem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, as long as the—that puts the labor market in, in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The fact that it’s getting into balance due to declines in both supply and demand, though, I think does—it is suggestive of downside risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re—of course, we’ll be watching that carefully.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Colby Smith with the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Two of your colleagues called for a quarter-point cut today, and I’m wondering what aspects of their argument were most compelling to you and how you are weighing their views against those on the Committee who, as of the June forecast, were in the camp of the Fed holding interest rates steady for the remainder of the year.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And, and just in terms of the June SEP in particular, is that still the best representation of where the core of the Committee is?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So on, on the dissents, you know, what you—what you want from everybody and also from a dissenter is a clear explanation for—of what your thinking is and what are the arguments you’re making.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—we had that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, basically, this was—this was quite a good meeting all around the table where people were—you know, thought carefully about this and put their positions out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, you know, the, the—sort of the majority of the Committee was of the view that inflation’s a bit above target, maximum employment is at target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That calls for modestly restrictive—in my way of thinking, a modestly restrictive stance of policy for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we had two dissenters who, I think—you know, you want that clear thinking and, and, and, you know, expression of your thinking, and we certainly had that today, I think all around the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of—you asked about the June SEP. You know, I wouldn’t—you’re right that that’s what it—that’s what it says, and that may—that may well—I, I couldn’t point to it six weeks later as, as expressing people’s thought—you really can’t do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t run an SEP, and I don’t like to substitute in my own estimate of what the SEP might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’ll just say that, you know, we, we haven’t made any decisions about September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll be monitoring all the incoming data and asking ourselves whether the federal funds rate is in the right place.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And, just on the point about policy being only modestly restrictive, does that mean that there’s actually not much scope to reduce rates once the conditions for a cut are met, barring a significant weakening of the labor market?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me say, my own estimate is modestly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there are—there are a range of views of what the neutral rate is at this moment for, for our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so others may say it’s more restrictive or less restrictive even.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re—we’re going to be—at some point, when we return to moving toward a more neutral stance, we’ll be making that judgment as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think we have a preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not so mechanical as saying, you know, “We’ve derived with great confidence the neutral rate, and that is our destination,” because, really, we understand that no one actually knows what the neutral rate is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know it by its works, and that will be how—the way the economy reacts over time to—you know, to slightly looser policy.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos, the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chair Powell, my question is about, what have you learned over the last few months about the inflation-generating and price pass-through process?

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: And just to drill down: The June CPI report showed evidence of tariff-induced goods inflation.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Now the tariff landscape is only starting to be settled with some of these more recent deals.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Given the lags between when tariffs are announced and when they show up in goods prices, is two months a long enough horizon to evaluate the impact and be confident that tariffs aren’t impacting the broader inflation process?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think you have to think of this as still quite early days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I think what we’re seeing now is substantial amounts of tariff revenue being collected, on the order of $30 billion a month, which is, you know, substantially higher than, than before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the evidence seems to be, mostly not paid, but paid only to a small extent, through exporters lowering their price.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And companies or retailers, sort of people who are upstream—institutions that are upstream from the consumer, are paying most of this for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumers are—it’s starting to show up in consumer prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you know, in the June report, we expect to see more of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we know from surveys that companies feel that they have every intention of, of, of putting this through to the consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, the truth is, they may not be able to in many cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it’s—we’re just going to have to watch and learn empirically how much of this and over what period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’ve learned that the process will probably be slower than, than expected at the beginning, but we never expected it to be fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think we have a long way to go to really understand exactly how we’ll be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how we’re thinking of it right now.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: So if I could follow up, is the reticence to “look through” core goods inflation being driven by the judgment that during the pandemic, expectations proved more adaptive than anyone at the Fed expected?

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Is it being driven by uncertainty over how restrictive policy is?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You could argue we are, a bit, “looking through” goods inflation by not raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we haven’t reacted to, to new inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, I mean, I wouldn’t—I wouldn’t insist upon that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I don’t think—I think the base case—I said—as I said, a reasonable base case is that these are one-time—one-time price effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, in the end, there, there will not be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This will not turn out to be inflation, because we’ll make sure that it’s not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will, through our tools, make sure that this does not move from being a one-time price increase to serious inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to do that efficiently, though, efficiently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that means we want to do it—if you—if you move too soon, you wind up maybe not getting inflation all the way fixed, and you have to come back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s inefficient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you move too late, you might do too—unnecessary damage to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there won’t be, in the end, a big inflationary problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we’re trying to do is accomplish that in a way that is efficient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in the end, there should be no doubt that we will do what we need to do to keep inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Ideally, we do it efficiently.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Michael.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Michael McKee from Bloomberg Television and Radio.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: The One Big Bill, leaving aside the adjectives—do you expect it to add stimulus to the economy in 2026?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: And would that be an argument for remaining on hold or cutting back on the number of rate cuts you would expect for next year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, of course, let me just—ritual disclaimer that we don’t express any judgments or anything, right, on, on fiscal legislation or other legislation, for that matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say, when you think that, you know, the biggest part of the bill was, was making permanent existing law on, on taxes, I don’t think we see it as particularly stimulative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There should be some stimulative effect, but it shouldn’t be significant over the next couple of years.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: And to follow up, what do you—well, I don’t want to put this in terms of you and the President, so let me ask it this way: Do you have concerns about the cost to the government of keeping rates elevated for longer in terms of interest rate charges?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, that’s—you know, we, we have a mandate, and that’s maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it is—it’s not something we do, to consider the cost to the government of our rate changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to be able to look at the goal variables Congress has given us—use the tools they have given us to achieve those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—we don’t consider the fiscal needs of the federal government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No advanced-economy central bank does that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it wouldn’t be good for—if we did do that, it would be good neither for our credibility nor for the credibility of U.S. fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s just not something we, we take into consideration.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Hi.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Victoria Guida with Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: When it comes to the renovations of the Federal Reserve’s headquarters that the Administration has been looking into, do you see their interest in that issue as being directly tied to the President’s push to get you to lower interest rates?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not for me to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will say, we had a—we had a nice visit with the President.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was an honor to host him.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something that happens very often at the Federal Reserve—to have the President come over, let alone to visit a building—but it was—it was a good visit.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Are there any aspects of the project that they’ve raised that you see as making you reconsider any aspects of the project?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we—this project was hatched and conceived almost a decade ago now, and we went through the very long process of clearing it through historic preservation at the National Capital Planning Commission and a lot of back-and-forth there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was very constructive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We started out to do the work, and we’re very well along on that work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I was quite pleased to have the President say multiple times that what he really wanted to see was, was us getting this construction completed as soon as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is our focus, and that’s what we’re going to do.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Andrew.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Andrew Ackerman with the Washington Post.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: What message do you take from the fact that inflation hit 2.1 percent last September and has bounced higher since?

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Why do you think financial conditions are restrictive and in neutral rates below 4 percent when inflation has stopped falling for almost a year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So inflation—when you talk about these 12-month inflation measures, you’re always battling residual seasonality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll have, for example, two months of high inflation, sometimes early in the year, and then inflation turns lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And a lot of that may just be an artifact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s why we look at the 12-month numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—look, I think inflation is most of the way back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are things like the catch-up inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, for example, all the insurance costs that are now—they’re only now going through inflation, but they actually reflect inflationary pressures from two, three years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s—that’s got to go through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, now we have, you know, three- or four-tenths of inflation in core inflation from tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and we, we, we can’t really separate that out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not going to have a separate, you know, kind of inflation that isn’t the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re always going to be dealing with the whole—all of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we—the composition, as I mentioned, has really changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, if you go back to the last couple of years, it was all about services inflation, which was being very sticky.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now services inflation is coming down nicely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Goods inflation was well behaved before, and now goods inflation is going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the story has really changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s partially because of tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also partially because we had restrictive policy in place, and we—and we’ve seen that—the result of that gradually work its way through the services economy.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Okay.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: The other thing I wanted to ask is, are you comfortable that BLS can continue performing their mission effectively if they take an 8 percent reduction in head count and authorized spending, as the Administration has proposed?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not going to comment on the Administration’s proposal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I do think—as I’ve said, I think that we—you know, we’re, we’re getting the data that we need to do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think it’s really important that, that good data helps not just the Fed—it helps the government, but it also helps the private sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people in the economy—they, they use this data a lot, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s quite important for our economy and, certainly, for the Fed’s work and other government agencies’ work that we—that we continue to get better at data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’ve been doing for 100 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been getting better and better and better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very hard to accurately capture in real time the output of a $20-plus trillion economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the United States has been a leader in that for 100 years, and we really need to continue that, in my view.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence from Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: How concerned are you, with, with the data that we’re showing—coming in showing no significant upward trend in inflation over the past six months, that the wait-and-see approach for inflation is actually giving companies cover to raise prices?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: How concerned am I that the—say that again.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: That the wait-and-see approach is getting— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: The wait-and-see approach—what do you mean by that?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: For, for cutting rates.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: You’re waiting to see if the tariffs will affect inflation.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So it’s a wait-and-see approach so that— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Well, so that—you know, that would—that’s where we’re—policy’s restrictive.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: When we start cutting, it’ll go toward neutral.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Okay.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: This delay, though, where you’re saying it’s a one-time—one-time price increase for tariffs, which they—which possibly could lead into bigger inflation or more inflation, is that giving companies cover, though, to raise prices?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, what, what may be giving—it’s not our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What may be giving—some companies will certainly be taking advantage of the fact of the tariffs and all of the discussion of how they’re going to—you know, companies will raise prices when and as they can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you—so you saw it famously in the—in the—in the first Administration of President Trump, during those tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Washing machines were tariffed, but, but, but dryers weren’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what do you know?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Price—the price of dryers went up, too, just like washing machines.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So companies will often just take—they’ll cross the street in a group, if you know what I mean.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’ll happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t see a lot of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, what we see now is basically the very beginnings of whatever the effects turn out to be on goods inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I’ll say again, they may be—they may be less than, than people estimate or more than people estimate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re not going to be zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumers will pay some of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Businesses will pay some of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Retailers will pay some of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we’re just going to have to, to see it through.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: And just a follow-up, if I could.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Some additional tariffs have been in place since February, and things, you know, really haven’t broken yet with the economy.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So how, how do you justify to somebody who’s looking for a house, who’s facing a 7 percent mortgage and maybe can’t afford those rates?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: How do you justify that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, so the housing—the housing is a—is a special case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our—we don’t set—we don’t set mortgage rates at the Fed, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We set an overnight rate, and the rates that go into mortgages are longer-term rates, like Treasury rates—it might be 30-year rates, it might be shorter than that, but it’s not the overnight Fed’s rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not that we don’t have any effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do have an effect, but we’re not the main effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are other things go—though, going on in the housing sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And one of those is just, there’s kind of a long-term housing shortage that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t built enough housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is not something the Fed can help with, but then that’ll be the case even after things normalize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I think the best thing that we can do for housing is to have 2 percent inflation and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s the—that’s what we can contribute to housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are lots of other jobs to do for the private sector and Congress, but that’s what we’re trying to get to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, I mean, we’ve made a lot of progress toward that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re in—we have a very good labor market right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation—we were very close to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re seeing some goods inflation move us away but, so far, not very far away.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Chris.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Well, can you give us a little more about, what kind of economic data does the Fed need to see before you’ll be ready to cut?

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: I mean, do you need inflation back nearly to target?

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Are there other things in the pricing that you look for?

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Do you need to see weakening in the job market?

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: What kind of things are you looking for?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, ultimately, it’s—it could be any—it could be any of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, but, you know, if you saw that the risks to the two goals were moving into balance, if they were fully in balance, that would imply that you should move toward a more—a more neutral stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is—this is the special situation we’re in, which is, we have two-sided risk, risk to both of our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When we paused, inflation was above target, and the labor market was pretty good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so, you know, that was a time when policy—policy was restrictive when we paused.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And to be restrictive is to be—to be supporting a return to our inflation target, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So as the two targets get back into balance, you would—you would think you’d move in, in, in a way closer to neutral and that the next—the next steps that we take are likely to be in that direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What will it take?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’ll just take—it’ll be the totality of the evidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, there’s quite a lot of data coming in, which, before the next meeting, will it be dispositive of that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—you know, it’s really hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t make those decisions right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll have to see.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Well, I guess just in terms of inflation, though, for example, like, will, will you—some people would point to, if it remains only in goods and it doesn’t bleed over to services, then maybe that’s evidence that the tariff effect is going to be a temporary, one-time thing.

speaker: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER
sentence: Is that kind of thing affect your thinking, or do you just need to see the number come down—closer to 2?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think—we’ll, we’ll, we’ll look at everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s—as I mentioned, you know, a pretty reasonable base case is that this will be a one-time price increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, in the end, we’ll make sure that that’s the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re just trying to do that efficiently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re—and “efficiently” means getting the timing right so we don’t—again, if we go—if we cut rates too soon, maybe we didn’t finish the job with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s—history is dotted with examples of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you cut too late, then maybe you’re doing unnecessary damage to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re trying to—we’re trying to get that timing right, and that’s effectively what we’re doing.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones, Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Just a question on the dollar.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: We’ve seen it decline quite heavily this year.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: I was wondering if there’s been any discussion about that at the meetings and how—to what degree that might be complicating your attempts to get inflation back to target.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this goes back to the division of labor between the Fed and the Treasury—as you, I’m sure, know—and, you know, the, the, the Treasury only speaks to the—speaks to the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not—it’s not something that’s been a topic of, of, you know, major discussion at all at, at—at the—at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I won’t say it doesn’t come up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The [FOMC meeting] transcripts, when they come out in a few years—they’ll probably reflect some mentions of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it would never be a, a major focus.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: And just to follow on, if I may, to Andrew’s question, I think the amount of imputed data in CPI now is up to 35 percent.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: I mean, is there any discussion of that as well?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Is there any consideration of looking at—into alternative measures, data scraping and so on, in order to just ensure you’ve got a good read on what’s happening to prices in the U.S. economy?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, we’re—so we’re monitoring the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do, of course—I mean, as you know, during the pandemic, we looked at a whole lot of new kinds of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People are looking at big data sets that you can get from all sorts of places.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do all of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But at the same—we really need—the government data really is the gold standard in data, and we need it to be—you know, to be good and be able to rely on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re not going to be able to substitute for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if—we have to make do with what we have, but I certainly hope that we get what we need.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jay O’Brien.

speaker: JAY O’BRIEN
sentence: Hi, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: JAY O’BRIEN
sentence: Jay O’Brien, ABC News.

speaker: JAY O’BRIEN
sentence: President Trump has obviously invoked your name a lot.

speaker: JAY O’BRIEN
sentence: He has personally pressured you.

speaker: JAY O’BRIEN
sentence: Are you concerned the way that conduct might impact the Fed’s independence going forward?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll just say that—so I, I think that having an independent central bank has been an institutional arrangement that has served the public well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as long as it serves the public well, it should continue and be respected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If it didn’t serve the public well, then, then it wouldn’t be something that we should just automatically defend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what it gives us and other central banks—what it gives you is the ability to make these, these very challenging decisions that—in ways that are focused on the data and the evolving outlook, the balance of risks, and all the things we talk about, and not political factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so governments all over the advanced-economy world have chosen to put a little bit of distance between direct political control of those decisions and the decisionmakers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you—if you were—if you weren’t—if you were not to have that, that would be a great temptation, of course, to, to use interest rates to affect elections, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s something that, that we don’t want to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that’s pretty widely understood.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Certainly, it is in Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, I mean—I mean, I think it’s very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll just say that.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Maria Eloisa.

speaker: MARIA ELOISA CAPURRO
sentence: Afternoon, Chair Powell.

speaker: MARIA ELOISA CAPURRO
sentence: Maria Eloisa Capurro from Bloomberg News.

speaker: MARIA ELOISA CAPURRO
sentence: You mentioned a slowdown in consumer spending, and I wanted to see if you could “walk us through” what was the discussion with the Committee around that.

speaker: MARIA ELOISA CAPURRO
sentence: We’ve seen delinquency rates rising for upper-income households.

speaker: MARIA ELOISA CAPURRO
sentence: How do you see that evolving in the next few months, and how much of a vulnerability that is for the economy going forward?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending had been very, very strong for the last couple of years and had—repeatedly, forecasters, not just us, had been forecasting it would slow down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now maybe it finally has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say, you know, if you talk to credit card companies, for example, they will tell you that the consumer is in solid shape and that spending is at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not growing rapidly, but it’s at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And delinquencies are not, not a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You mentioned high-end delinquencies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know what to make of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I read the same thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—so, generally—and if you look at the banks and when the banks talk about in their earnings calls, their—the performance of credit has been good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, essentially, you, you have a consumer that’s in good shape and is spending, not at a rapid rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it, it, it’s true.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it was, again, right in line with what we expected, the GDP data that we got this week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and I think it’s still a little bit difficult to interpret, because you have these massive swings in net exports, which, which may also be affecting—you know, some of that can be affected by—can affect consumer spending as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Look, we—it’s one of the data points that we pay most careful attention to, and there’s no question that it’s slowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re watching it closely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we also watch the labor market and the performance of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those are our two—those are our two variables that we’re assigned to maximize.

speaker: MARIA ELOISA CAPURRO
sentence: And just to follow up on what my colleagues were asking about the dissents: Governor Waller said that the labor market is on edge, and he was pointing to weaknesses on the private sector.

speaker: MARIA ELOISA CAPURRO
sentence: I was wondering, you’ve said that the main number to look at is the unemployment number overall, but what was the discussion about the state of the private jobs market?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m not going to talk about any individual’s—you know, any individual’s comments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, look, I think what we know is that private-sector job creation, you know, certainly in the last report—we’ll see on Friday—but had come down a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and if you—if you take the QCEW adjustment seriously, with it—it may be even low—maybe close to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the unemployment rate is still—was still low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, what that’s telling you is that, that, you know, demand for workers is slowing, but so is the supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s a—it’s in balance, oddly enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got a very low unemployment rate, and it’s kind of been there for a year as job creation has moved down, but also we know that, you know, because of immigration policy really, the flow into our labor forces is just a great deal slower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those two things have slowed more or less in tandem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at things, like I mentioned, quits, look at wages—wages are gradually cooling—look at vacancies to unemployment, those things have been pretty stable for—they haven’t really moved a lot in a full year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think if you take the totality of the labor market data, you’ve got a solid labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think you have to see that there are downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not—you don’t see weakening in the labor market, but I think you’ve got downside risks in a world where unemployment’s being held down because both demand and supply are declining.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that’s—it’s worth paying close attention to it, and we are.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nancy.

speaker: NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER
sentence: Nancy Marshall-Genzer with Marketplace.

speaker: NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER
sentence: One more question on the lack of unanimity in today’s decision, the two dissents.

speaker: NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER
sentence: Was there talk during the meeting?

speaker: NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER
sentence: I know you’re not going to talk about what—exactly what individuals said, but, in general, was there talk during the meeting of cutting rates, and what was the case against that at the meeting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we have—we have an economic go-round, where people talk about the economy, and then the next—to—then to—that’s yesterday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then today, we have a monetary policy go-round, all the way around the table—everyone gives their views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the discussion around policy was—the majority view was, was still what it has been, which is that inflation is running above target, maximum employment is right at target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That means policy, policy should be a little bit restrictive, somewhat restrictive, because we want—we want inflation to, to move all the way back to its target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s where people have been and still are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Two of our members felt that the time had come to cut and that they—for the reasons that they’re—they’re going to express.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I won’t tell you the reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They—they’ll issue some kind of a—of a thing in the next day or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but that’s the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say, you know, well argued, very thoughtfully argued all around the table, good arguments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, it’s a situation where—an unusual situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is in—is in, you know, good shape, but it’s an unusual situation where you have risks to both your employment mandate and your inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the nature of a supply shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s probably not surprising that there would be differences and different perspectives on that as well as different views of where the neutral rate is, so they—different views of how tight policy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will say, what you hope is that people, you know, explain their, their positions very thoughtfully and clearly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we absolutely had that today all the way around the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would call it one of the better meetings I can recall from that standpoint.

speaker: NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER
sentence: And you’ve said you’re waiting to be confident inflation is heading toward your 2 percent target before you start cutting rates.

speaker: NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER
sentence: When you do get that confidence, would you be in—would you be in favor of lowering rates right away?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not, not quite the way I would put it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I said that’s why we think policy should, should be restrictive, is because, you know, inflation is above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When we—when we have risks to both goals—one of them is farther away from goal than the other, and that’s inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Maximum employment’s at goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you have to—that means policy should be tight because tight policy is what brings inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you came to the view that the risks to the two were more in balance, that would imply that policy shouldn’t be restrictive, it should be more neutral—more, more, you know, a neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that would be somewhat lower than where we are now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one knows exactly where that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—that’s the framework I think I’d be taking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’ll just have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to be obviously looking at a lot of data in the next cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is one of the cycles where we have two employment and two inflation reports, and we’ll see where that takes us.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jeff Cox.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for taking the question.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: Jeff Cox from CNBC.com.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: A metric that you like to cite a lot is the final sales to private domestic purchasers.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: That was down to a 1.2 percent gain in the second quarter from 1.9 percent in Q1, suggesting that there’s some softening in underlying demand.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: Just wondering if you look at that and you combine that with some of the housing numbers that—with the weakness that you acknowledge at the top of your remarks—that the housing market is, in fact, weak.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: And the inflation numbers from GDP today came down 2.1 percent for headline, 2.5 percent for core.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: I’m wondering how much more movement you would need to see from these data points before you would be comfortable with cutting in, say, September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s going to be the total—hard to answer that specifically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: PDFP, I think, for the first half—private domestic final purchases, or final sales, as people call it—was 1.6 on the first half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP, I believe, was 1.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the whole half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You mentioned the quarters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those are slower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, GDP is bumpy quarter to quarter, half to half, and often gets revised, you know, after the fact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market data, we, we still think, is—continue to think, is the best data we have on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that shows a 4.1 percent unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It shows wages, you know, still at a healthy level, but moving ever closer to what we would regard as long-run sustainable, consistent with longer-run productivity and 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the labor market is actually still quite solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Even ignoring tariffs, it’s a little bit above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And tariffs—so we’re watching all of that and, again, trying to—trying to do the right thing in what is a challenging situation, because you’re being pulled in two directions and you have to decide which of those it took to go in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, actually, at some point, if they’re—if they’re sort of equally at risk, then you really want to be at a neutral policy stance, which we’re not right now.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: So it’d be safe to say that, if the data kind of stays in line with where it is right now, that you wouldn’t be comfortable with cutting in September?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not going to—I’m not going to say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I, I just think we’re going to need to see the data, and it can go in many different directions—the inflation data and, and the employment data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll just—we’re going to make a judgment based on all of the data and based on that balance-of-risks analysis that I mentioned.

speaker: JEFF COX
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Greg Robb, for the last question.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: Greg Robb from MarketWatch.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: The Treasury Secretary has said recently that it would be confusing for the markets if you stayed on as a Governor after your term on the—as Chair ends.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: And I was wondering if you had any update for us on—a decision on that front.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sorry, I do not have any update for you.

sentence: Thanks very much, everyone.
